sources.citation: Robinson, Stuart. 2011. Split intransitivity in Rotokas, a Papuan language of Bougainville. PhD dissertation, Radboud Universiteit Nijmegen (MPI Series in Psycholinguistics 61).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Phonology chapter is on Rotokas only. On Keriaka: 'Eivo and Keriaka are completely undocumented' (p. 17); Table 2.4 (p. 23) lists 'Keriaka kjx 1,000 UNDESCRIBED'; p. 103 n.12 calls Eivo, Keriaka, Rapoisi 'almost entirely undocumented sister languages'. Reproduces Allen & Hurd 1963 cognate percentages (p. 23). Nothing on Keriaka stress.

sources.citation: Tryon, Darrell. 2005. The languages of Bougainville. In A. J. Regan & H. M. Griffin (eds.), Bougainville before the conflict, 31-46. Canberra: Pandanus Books / ANU Press.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Lists Keriaka (W Bougainville, 1,000 speakers [1981]) with name variants from Allen & Hurd 1963, Wurm & Hattori 1981-83 and Ethnologue 2000, and places it in Wurm's West Bougainville Stock / Ross's North Bougainville group. No phonology, no stress.

sources.citation: Dunn, Michael, Ger Reesink & Angela Terrill. 2002. The East Papuan languages: a preliminary typological appraisal. Oceanic Linguistics 41(1): 1-36.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Keriaka appears only in the classification figure (p. 2); it is not in the typological sample (Glottolog tags the paper for Taulil, Kuot, Anem, Ata, Sulka, Motuna, Baining, Lavukaleve, Lusi, Touo, Aiwoo). Nothing on Keriaka stress.

sources.note: 'Keriaka and Eivo, both on Bougainville, are omitted because I had no data.' No phonology, no stress.

sources.citation: Wurm, Stephen A. 1975. The East Papuan Phylum in general. In S. A. Wurm (ed.), New Guinea Area Languages and Language Study Vol. 1: Papuan languages and the New Guinea linguistic scene (Pacific Linguistics C-38), 783-804. Canberra: ANU.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Keriaka appears only as a 'family-level isolate' (1000 speakers) in the West Bougainville Stock (p. 795). The only prosodic remark is stock-level and about Rotokas: 'in Rotokas at least, there is a complex suprasegmental phonology in which length and stress patterns play a part' (p. 796). Nothing on Keriaka stress.
